lesson_title: Salt Shatters, Copper Bends: Three Bonds Explain Everything
hook_text: Hit salt with a hammer and it EXPLODES into fragments. Hit copper and it just... dents. Why?
clip_script: Why does table salt sit as a brittle crystal that dissolves in water, candle wax as a soft solid that slumps on a hot day, and copper as a shiny metal that bends and conducts? Because their atoms are held together in three different ways. Salt is a swap: sodium hands its unwanted electron to chlorine, both become charged ions, and plus-minus attraction stacks them into a rigid grid millions deep. Knock the grid and a layer slides — plus meets plus — and the crystal tears itself apart. That is why salt shatters. Wax is a share: non-metal atoms pool electron pairs into strong little molecules — but the molecules barely grip each other, so warmth lets them slide. That is why wax slumps. Copper is a pool: every atom tosses its outer electrons into one communal sea washing around a lattice of positive kernels. Bend the wire and the sea just flows around the new arrangement — the bonding survives. That is why metal dents instead of dying. And the sea is already mobile, which is why the lamp lights the instant you flick the switch. Three bonds. Three personalities. One glance at the periodic table tells you which story any substance is living.
visual_style: Triptych of macro scenes: a salt crystal fracturing along glowing plus-minus grid lines, wax molecules sliding like beads in warm light, and a copper wire bending while a blue electron sea streams around fixed golden kernels.
mood: Satisfying materials-science reveal — everyday objects explained from the atoms up.
pacing: Hammer-hit open, three quick chapters with a beat each, closing on the periodic-table one-glance rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any substance's story straight off the table.
